title: Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act
summary: When the IRS seeks information about you from a third party, current law requires it to notify you before making contact — but not to spell out the specific information it’s seeking. This bill requires the IRS — when the information relates to determining your tax liability, has not been previously requested from you, and could reasonably be provided by you — to identify each specific item of information it intends to seek from the third party, and to give you at least 45 days to respond before it makes contact. One exception applies: this itemized-notice requirement does not apply if the Secretary determines the third-party information is necessary.
brief: Requires the IRS to tell taxpayers exactly what information it plans to seek from third parties and give them at least 45 days to respond first.

top_lines.headline: Specific Notice Required
subs: IRS must itemize third-party info related to tax liability that the taxpayer wasn’t asked for and could provide
Taxpayers get at least 45 days to respond — more if they request it with reasonable cause

top_lines.headline: Secretary Necessity Exception
subs: Itemized-notice requirement waived if the Secretary determines the third-party information is necessary

likelihoodReason: Only 1 cosponsor and a narrow taxpayer privacy focus. The IRS exemption allowing the Secretary to waive specificity requirements whenever deemed necessary limits the bill's practical effect, which may reduce the urgency Senate sponsors attach to it. IRS procedural reform bills without broad coalition backing rarely advance quickly in the Senate.

items.main: Names the Act the “Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Specificity of Third-Party Contact Notices

items.main: Amends Section 7602(c)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to require the IRS to identify each specific item of information it intends to seek from a third party when that information is related to determining tax liability, has not been previously requested from the taxpayer, and could reasonably be provided by the taxpayer.
items.detail: Under the amended subparagraph (C), the IRS must — except as otherwise provided by the Secretary — provide the taxpayer with reasonable opportunity and a period of not less than 45 days (or more, if the taxpayer requests additional time and shows reasonable cause) to respond before contact is made with the third party. A new exception at Section 7602(c)(3)(B) provides that the itemized-notice requirement (subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1)) does not apply to information sought from a person other than the taxpayer if the Secretary determines that such information is necessary. The amendments apply to notices provided under section 7602(c) after the date that is 12 months after enactment.

underreported.summary: The bill’s itemized-notice requirement does not apply whenever the Secretary determines that the third-party information is necessary, with no standard stated for what makes information necessary and no procedural check on that determination.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed as expanding taxpayer notification rights, but the necessity exception lets the IRS skip the itemized-notice requirement based on the Secretary’s determination that the information is necessary, with no defined standard, independent review, or notice to the taxpayer that the exception was invoked.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steube
featured_quotes.text: At its core, this commonsense legislation is a simple due process idea: Before the IRS goes to your bank, your employer, your vendor, or another third party for information about you, when you can reasonably provide that information yourself, you should be told what they are looking for and given a fair chance to respond. Under current law, taxpayers can receive a general third-party contact notice, but too often those notices aren't specific enough to let a person meaningfully respond.

gaps: The bill requires the IRS to give the taxpayer 45 days to respond but does not specify whether the IRS is barred from contacting the third party if the taxpayer provides the requested information within the window.

The bill does not address the taxpayer's right to receive notice that the Secretary has invoked the necessity exception, leaving taxpayers without information about why the standard procedure was not followed.

added: Section 7602(c)(1)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code — requirement that the IRS identify each specific item of information sought from a third party when that information is related to determining tax liability, has not been previously requested from the taxpayer, and could reasonably be provided by the taxpayer

Section 7602(c)(3)(B) — exception providing that the new itemized-notice requirement does not apply to information sought from a person other than the taxpayer if the Secretary determines that such information is necessary
modified: Redesignated subparagraph (C) of section 7602(c)(1) amended to require, except as otherwise provided by the Secretary, a period of not less than 45 days (or more, if the taxpayer requests additional time and shows reasonable cause) to respond before third-party contact

New specificity duty narrowed — the IRS must itemize info sought from third parties only when it "is related to determining tax liability" (plus the existing not-previously-requested and taxpayer-could-provide tests)

Exception for the Secretary simplified — the specificity rule now does not apply whenever "the Secretary determines that such information is necessary," replacing the two-prong carve-out (collection of a tax liability, or necessity notwithstanding taxpayer availability)
removed: Dropped the phrase letting taxpayers respond "including by providing the information described in subparagraph (B)" from the 45-day response window
Removed the standalone exception for information sought "with respect to the collection of a tax liability"
